analysis.one_liner: Bans banks from charging non-customers a surcharge to use their ATMs.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban ATM surcharges got a committee hearing but never came up for a Senate vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, banks increasingly charged people a fee for using another bank's ATM — a surcharge on top of whatever their own bank charged. This bill would have amended the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to make those surcharges illegal whenever a person uses an ATM belonging to a bank where they hold no account, through a national or regional ATM network. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a hearing but never voted to send it to the full Senate, and the Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who withdraws cash from an ATM that is not their own bank's. They would no longer pay the owner-bank's surcharge, and the ban would cover transactions routed through national and regional ATM networks, which is how nearly all out-of-network withdrawals work.

how_it_helps.text: Defines an 'electronic terminal surcharge' as a fee charged by the bank that owns or operates the ATM.

Prohibits that surcharge whenever the transaction does not involve an account at the ATM-owner bank and runs through a national or regional electronic banking network — meaning a customer of Bank A could use Bank B's machine without paying Bank B a fee.

analysis.who_pays: Banks that own ATMs would lose the surcharge revenue they collect from non-customers, and would have to cover the cost of operating those machines from other income.

drawbacks.text: Banks could argue that running and restocking off-site ATMs costs money, and that without surcharges some banks would install fewer machines in low-traffic or rural locations, leaving consumers with fewer convenient machines even if the ones they find are free.

The ban is one-sided: it stops the ATM-owner's surcharge but does not stop a consumer's own bank from charging a separate out-of-network fee, so customers could still face some cost for using another bank's machine.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For everyday consumers the benefit is direct and easy to see: the fee they actually feel at the machine would disappear. The main honest cost is that banks, no longer able to charge outsiders for machine use, might place fewer ATMs in spots where few of their own customers use them. On balance the bill shifted a small, universal cost away from millions of bank customers and onto the banks that profit from the payment system.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held one hearing, but the committee never voted to send it to the full Senate and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 23, 1996 by Sen. D'Amato with five Democratic cosponsors, and read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee.
The Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill on July 11, 1996, its only action beyond the referral.
No further action was taken; the committee never reported the bill, the Senate never voted on it, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks that collect ATM surcharges from non-customers kept that revenue because the ban never became law; consumers kept paying out-of-network surcharges.

for.name: Sen. Alfonse D'Amato
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-NY), bill sponsor and chairman of the Senate Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Sens. John Kerry, Barbara Boxer, Richard Bryan, Carol Moseley-Braun, and Patty Murray
for.role: Democratic cosponsors from Massachusetts, California, Nevada, Illinois, and Washington

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on July 11, 1996, but never voted to report the bill to the full Senate.

against.name: Banking industry
against.role: Banks and ATM operators that earn surcharge revenue from non-customers
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to restrict or ban ATM surcharges, arguing fees pay for machine placement and operation.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors — and no vote was ever taken, so party divisions never appeared on the record.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate the surcharge banks charge non-customers at their machines, a fee borne by millions of ordinary bank customers. Banks' interest in keeping that revenue ran directly against the consumers paying it.
